name: User Feedback Loops and the Data Flywheel
question: Are users telling us what is broken, and do we act on it?
summary: Users show whether an answer helped far more often through behaviour than through ratings. A feedback loop captures explicit signals (thumbs, ratings, comments) and implicit ones (retries, rephrasing, copying the answer, abandoning, asking for a human, editing a draft), attaches them to the trace of the conversation, and turns them into work: a weekly triage clusters failures into patterns, each pattern becomes eval cases and a fix, and suitable examples become fine-tuning or preference data. That cycle of product use producing better data producing a better product is the data flywheel. Automated scoring of sampled traffic is covered by Online Evals; this technique is about the signals users give and the process that acts on them. Using conversations for training needs a lawful basis, such as notice and consent under India’s DPDP Act, and redaction.
useCases: Support and sales assistants with high conversation volume
Copilots where users edit drafts before sending
Any product whose eval set has stopped reflecting real use

items.detail: thumbs, ratings and comments; rare (1–3% of sessions) and skewed to strong feelings
retry, rephrase, copy, abandon, human handoff, edit distance on drafts
every signal joined to the conversation, prompt version and retrieved context
weekly review that clusters failures into named patterns with counts
days from a pattern appearing to a fix in production
patterns → eval cases, fixes and training data → measured release

steps: Log explicit and implicit signals with the trace id and prompt version
Review a weekly sample of negative signals and cluster them into failure patterns
Turn each pattern into eval cases, then a prompt, retrieval or tool fix
Add consented, redacted examples to training or preference data; measure the next release
pitfalls: Counting thumbs-down alone, which misses most failures
Collecting feedback with no owner or weekly review, so nothing changes
Training on conversations without notice, consent or redaction

steps.title: Capture explicit feedback
steps.text: Dak Mitra, a fictional logistics company, adds thumbs to its support chat. Only about 1.5% of 2 lakh weekly chats get a rating, mostly from very unhappy or very happy users.

steps.title: Capture what users do
steps.text: Retries, rephrasing, copying the tracking answer and asking for a human are logged as implicit signals on the same trace. They are noisy, but there are ten times more of them.

steps.title: Triage every week
steps.text: A reviewer samples 300 negative traces, clusters them and names the patterns: “COD refund status in Hinglish”, “pincode not serviceable”, “wrong courier partner”.

steps.title: Turn patterns into evals and fixes
steps.text: The top five patterns each add 20 eval cases and get an owner. A fix ships only when those cases pass.

steps.title: Feed the flywheel carefully
steps.text: Only conversations with training consent and clean redaction go to the training queue, in line with DPDP notice and consent.

steps.title: Measure the loop
steps.text: After eight weeks, first-contact resolution rises from 72% to 79%, and the time from a pattern appearing to its fix falls from 45 to 10 days.

cons: Linking signals to traces needs instrumentation
Training on user data needs consent and redaction
avoidWhen: Training on raw conversations without a lawful basis

practice.scenario: Dak Mitra, a fictional logistics company, handles 2 lakh support chats a week in English and Hinglish. Thumbs-down covered 1.5% of chats and showed a quarter of failures. It now logs retries, rephrasing and requests for a human on the same traces, a reviewer clusters 300 negative traces each week into named patterns, and the top five become eval cases, fixes with owners and, where customers consented, redacted training data. In eight weeks first-contact resolution rises from 72% to 79% and a failure pattern goes from first sighting to fix in 10 days instead of 45.

industries.use: Tracking, COD refunds and delivery complaints
Card and UPI dispute assistants where handoffs signal failure
Copilots where the edit distance on drafts shows quality

practice.analogy: A restaurant that reads the plates coming back to the kitchen, not just the comment cards, and changes one recipe each week based on what was left uneaten.

library.name: pandas
library.what: A few lines of pandas turn exported signals into a weekly failure-pattern table; any tracing tool can export them.

practice.note: signals.csv is an export from your tracing or analytics tool with one row per signal; the pattern column is filled by the reviewer during triage.

samples.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.read_csv("signals.csv", parse_dates=["ts"])        # trace_id, ts, kind, pattern
week = s[s.ts >= s.ts.max() - pd.Timedelta(days=7)]

negative = week[week.kind.isin(["thumbs_down", "retry", "rephrase", "handoff"])]
print("traces with a negative signal:", negative.trace_id.nunique())

table = (negative.dropna(subset=["pattern"])
         .groupby("pattern").trace_id.nunique()
         .sort_values(ascending=False).head(5))
print(table)                                              # top five failure patterns
table.to_csv("patterns_this_week.csv")

interview.question: How would you use user feedback to improve an assistant?
interview.answer: Capture explicit and implicit signals on traces, triage a sample of negative traces weekly into named failure patterns, turn each into eval cases and a fix with an owner, and add consented, redacted examples to training data; measure each release on the eval set.

interview.question: Why are implicit signals important?
interview.answer: Few users rate, and those who do are skewed to extremes. Retries, rephrasing, handoffs and edits are far more common and reveal failures users never report.
